newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian guerrillas free Uruguayan ambassador. [CORRECTED 15:50 GMT 26/12]
newsitem.headline: Peruvian guerrillas free Uruguayan ambassador. [CORRECTED 15:50 GMT 26/12]

text.p: Marxist guerrillas in Peru freed Uruguay's ambassador Tabare Bocalandro on Tuesday evening after a Uruguayan court denied a Peruvian extradition request and set two of their comrades free.

Chief Red Cross negotiators Michel Minnig said Bocalandro's release reduced the number of hostages still being held by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels in the Japanese ambassador's residence to 105.
Minnig made no comment on why Bocalandro had been released.

The two men walked slowly out of the residence side-by-side in a surprise twist to the hostage crisis. Bocalandro, his head bowed and still dressed in the elegant navy suit he wore to the Dec. 17 cocktail party stormed by guerrillas at the ambassador's home, was taken away in a police car to an unknown destination.

Earlier on Tuesday a Uruguayan appeals court ruled that two alleged MRTA members held in connection with the 1995 kidnapping of a Bolivian businessman in the Uruguayan capital of Montevideo be freed. (Corrects nationality of businessman)
The court ruling revoked a decision in May to uphold a Peruvian extradition request against Luis Alberto Samaniego and Silvia Gora Rivera.
Uruguayan officials insisted that the two events were not connected and that the two MRTA suspects were not being swapped for the ambassador's freedom.

"There is absolutely no connection between the release of these two prisoners and the situation of Ambassador Bocalandro," Ernesto Martinez Gariano, in charge of the Uruguayan embassy in Lima during Bocalandro's capture, told Peru's Panamericana television network.

Smaniego welcomed his release but said he was still wary of being re-arrested. "We still don't know if our freedom is uncondicional or...if they could arrest us again," he told Uruguay's Channel Four television network.
It was the first release from the besieged residence since 225 men were freed on Sunday night and briefly brightened an otherwise cheerless Christmas Eve for the hostages.

The rebels who stormed the elegant cocktail party at the ambassador's residence still hold six foreign ambassadors, two Peruvian government ministers, dozens of Japanese businessmen and the brother of Peru's President Alberto Fujimori.
